extracted.intended_audience: Public Information Officers, Incident Management Teams, and Agency Administrators responsible for incident/public information during all-hazards incidents
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and checklists for Public Information Officers and Agency Administrators to prepare for, plan, and respond to special (high-visibility or sensitive) incidents, including media handling, notifications, and interagency coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request help of more experienced Public Information Officers
rubrics_metrics.description: If the special situation is fairly serious and has the potential to generate a significant amount of public and news media interest, do not hesitate to request the help of more experienced Public Information Officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring in experienced PIOs early when potential public/media interest is significant; escalate staffing rather than attempting to handle alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know lead agency policies on special situations and information release
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step in preparing for special situations is to make sure that you know the lead agency’s policies with regard to handling special situations and the release of information to the news media and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some agencies want the Incident Management Team to handle special situations while others want local personnel; confirm which applies and follow lead agency policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss policy and establish role agreement with leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss the policy with the Public Information Officer to whom you report, or with the Incident Commander, or local Agency Administrator/Agency Official if you are the only Public Information Officer assigned to the incident. Reach an agreement ahead of time on what your role will be in the event of a special situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify delegation of authority and reporting relationships in advance so roles and responsibilities are understood during the incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a plan: Assess the incident
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the incident before planning how to handle the special situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider: scale of the incident; what is happening regionally/nationally and significance of this area; how rare this type of incident is; visibility of the incident; expected duration; jurisdictional issues; who is affected and whether prominent people will gain media attention; proximity to news media; competing news stories; whether an investigation has been initiated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a plan: Assess the staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess available staff resources and capabilities to handle the incident-within-an-incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: Do I need to request another PIO? Do I have enough people? Do I have the right levels of experience? Can these people give interviews? Do they have necessary skills? Do I need to order more people?

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a plan: Make assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Address and assign specific audiences and internal tasks as they pertain to the plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make assignments for: media, public, politicians, incident personnel and other internal audiences. Also assess facilities (size, communications, location, accessibility) as part of assignment planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan considerations (policies, approvals, and related subjects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects the Special Situations Plan should take into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include agency policies; release approvals (e.g., releasing accident victims’ names or identifying characteristics); home base communication (keep home base informed if away); conflicts between agencies and/or the public; rumors and monitoring media and social media; evacuations (procedures, approvals); VIP visits; and any other approvals or coordination requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write and update the plan regularly
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularly update the Special Situations Plan and review it at least once each Operational Period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the plan as a living document; change as needed based on operational feedback and evolving circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitating media interviews: sensitivity and preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sensitive when speaking with victims, witnesses, survivors, and other audiences during interviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand some people want to talk and some want privacy; work with local PIO/PAO; respect local customs; ask 'What are the sensitive issues?'; ensure HIPAA compliance; prepare witnesses/survivors for what they cannot talk about; be ready to help exit difficult interview situations; recognize legal restrictions on who can speak; gently obtain a written fact sheet from family to initially satisfy media; know your agency policy and delegation of authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental sensing
rubrics_metrics.description: Environmental sensing is a public relations practice of understanding what is going on in the world that may be pertinent to the incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know current and recent media coverage and unrelated stories that affect coverage of your incident; consider political, social, and environmental context (e.g., testimony or promises that make your incident more newsworthy). Incidents occur in broader contexts that influence how they are managed and how information is received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling injuries and fatalities: withholding identifying information until next of kin notified
rubrics_metrics.description: Public Information Officers must never release the names or other identifying characteristics of incident personnel or the public injured or killed during an incident until the next of kin have been notified and the Incident Commander or proper authority has given permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If media learn of injuries/fatalities first, ask for patience while confirming; pursue confirmation immediately and return calls as soon as possible; never deny occurrence if they may have occurred; stand firm on withholding names until next-of-kin notification and authority permission; if permission is given but next-of-kin not notified, release only a brief account of how injuries/fatalities occurred while withholding names and identifying characteristics; if media has a name and notification is not confirmed, ask media to withhold publication until confirmation; contact hospitals/coroners/LE and seek cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling investigations: limit commentary and avoid speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the cause is well established and the Incident Commander gives permission, the IIC may release an approved statement about the cause. In all other cases, say the cause is under investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be pressured into releasing partial information or speculating about outcomes; offhand remarks can jeopardize investigations and interagency relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling evacuations: coordinate with law enforcement and ensure accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Evacuations are normally ordered by law enforcement agencies in coordination with the Incident Management Team; PIO must coordinate with the appropriate law enforcement agency to understand what evacuation information can be released.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If IIC is asked to release evacuation info, ensure the information is current and accurate; misinformation about evacuations can create panic and chaos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand agency policy and focus on releasable information
rubrics_metrics.description: The Public Information Officer must understand the agency policies under which they will operate, including differences between their agency and the lead agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss policy with the Incident Commander and Agency Administrator; discuss agency-specific procedures (e.g., media flights); focus on releasable information and refer to the Delegation of Authority; above all, use common sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Releasing confidential or inaccurate information: do not release
rubrics_metrics.description: Release of confidential information (such as names of juveniles) or release of inaccurate information (such as incorrect evacuation sites) can jeopardize investigations and cause harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not release such information; avoid unnecessary embarrassment to agencies and individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public record information: types considered public and releasable
rubrics_metrics.description: There are types of public record information that are considered public and releasable to the media and public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be familiar with what is public versus non-releasable in your jurisdiction and agency policy; consult the Delegation of Authority and legal advisors as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incident information not releasable (notifications and investigations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The guidance lists incident information that is not releasable: Victims’ names (know the agency’s policy), aircraft characteristics, home unit, suspects’ names (students/minors), medical records and information, performance records, investigative information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memorize or keep this list accessible; coordinate with investigative agencies before releasing any potentially sensitive details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate and work directly with law enforcement on crime-scene incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: The PIO will work with law enforcement directly (IMTs bring their own) at a crime scene; local law enforcement will usually conduct its own information gathering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be in direct contact with law enforcement and coordinate releases; expect law enforcement to have their own PIO and procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit responses to operational/logistical questions and refer legal/investigative/medical questions
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked about complex or sensitive events (e.g., arrests, accidents, protester motives, alleged criminal activity), answer routine operational questions but do not handle investigative, legal, medical, or motive-based questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of acceptable answers: how teams are hired, what they do, strategy, number of cleanup workers, known facts (time/general location/number of fatalities), purpose of a flight. Examples of off-limit questions: how sheriff knew the immigration status, what will happen to arrestees, next-of-kin details, specific nature of injuries, cause of crash before investigation, allegations' motives. Refer such questions to the appropriate agency (Sheriff's Department, Immigration Service, hospital, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Accident Investigation Team, FAA) AFTER you verify the spokesperson and their willingness to take calls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare and use key messages
rubrics_metrics.description: Use concise, pre-crafted key messages appropriate to the situation to communicate sympathy, roles, and facts without speculating or assigning blame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: express condolences; stress responders' role and training; emphasize safety concerns; note that investigations are underway; explain what is known and what is not; acknowledge heroic efforts. Keep messages focused, empathetic, and fact-based.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify and refer to external spokespeople before directing media
rubrics_metrics.description: When referring media to other agencies (e.g., Sheriff’s Department, immigration, hospital, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service), verify the name and phone number of the willing spokesperson in advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Call ahead to confirm the spokesperson and that they are willing to handle media inquiries before sending media to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: BEFORE the incident: Agency Administrator preparedness checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency Administrators should take preparatory steps before a critical incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine likely incident types (fire, law enforcement, aviation, vehicle accident, etc.); identify agencies with statutory/jurisdictional responsibilities; pre-plan incident response and develop criteria for implementing ICS structure; prepare a Delegation of Authority for critical incident management; ensure all employees have current emergency notification information; identify family liaison(s); develop local emergency operating plan with initial response and notification procedures; provide training and exercises focused on interagency cooperation and incident management; ensure key personnel understand roles and are capable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency Notification and Reporting procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop contact lists and processes for reporting serious injuries, deaths, shelter deployments, and entrapments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop contact list for reporting (see Agency Reporting Log); identify processes for investigating and reporting; for wildland fire fatalities/entrapments notify National Interagency Coordination Center within 24 hours using NWCG Form PMS 405-1; ensure OSHA is notified within eight hours for specified events; establish next-of-kin notification protocols and coordinate with local authorities (see Fatality/Serious Injury Notification Guide).

rubrics_metrics.name: Family Liaison responsibilities and resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and prepare resources to assist designated family liaison(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify grief counselors, peer supporters, administrative support; identify internal policies (autopsy requirements for work-related death benefits, what death benefits are covered, procedures for personnel paperwork, advice for filing claims) and prepare liaison resources accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical Incident Stress Management (CISM) readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that CISM protocols and resources are identified prior to a critical incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify local/regional/area CISM resources (peer support, defusing, debriefing); contact them to discuss activation, capabilities, and costs; identify Employee Assistance Program (EAP) capabilities for grief counseling, family support, and critical incident stress support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information and Communications planning for critical incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop critical incident communication procedures as part of a local emergency operating plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include: agency jurisdictions; directory of local/regional/national support; directory of agency experts (qualified PIOs, crisis communication teams, experienced crisis communicators); key spokespersons; list of communication tools/resources; process for setting up a communication center; coordination of information dissemination; process to coordinate communications with accident investigation teams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create fact sheets, bios, media lists, and mapping/graphics support
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare communication products and supporting technical resources in advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create fact sheets and bio-sketches for agency and community; prepare generic formats for additional fact sheets and a glossary of terms; create media contact lists with phone/fax numbers; identify technical expertise to produce maps and graphics (directions for family visits, memorials, etc.).
